items.en: SpaceX just broke an uncharacteristically long Starlink launch drought.

The company sent 27 of its Starlink internet satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) today (Oct. 12), launching them atop a Falcon 9 rocket from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base at 8:28 p.m. EDT (5:28 p.m. local time; 0028 GMT on Oct. 13)

It was the first Starlink mission for a Falcon 9 since Sept. 19, which was another 27-satellite liftoff from Vandenberg. For some perspective on this recent gap: Between Aug. 19 and Sept. 6, a span of 19 days, SpaceX launched seven Starlink missions with Falcon 9s.

SpaceX did loft a batch of Starlinks after that, but it wasn't aboard a Falcon 9. The company's Starship megarocket carried 26 next-gen Starlink V3 craft on its 14th test flight, which took place on Sept. 28.

Starship reached orbit for the first time ever on Flight 14, and it deployed the Starlinks successfully as well. This will happen many more times going forward, if all goes to plan: The Starlink V3 constellation will eventually consist of about 100,000 satellites, all of which will fly on Starship, Elon Musk has said.

Indeed, SpaceX plans to sunset the Falcon 9 and its cousin, the Falcon Heavy, in the next few years, shifting their duties over to the fully reusable, far more powerful Starship, which remains in the test-flight phase.

That shift will be a big one for the spaceflight community, for the Falcon 9 is the workhorse rocket of its generation. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number as the rest of the world's orbital launchers combined. Nearly three-quarters of those Falcon 9 launches were Starlink missions.

Things have slowed down a bit in 2026. Today's flight was the 112th Falcon 9 liftoff of the year, and the 82nd in service of the Starlink megaconstellation, which currently consists of more than 11,100 active satellites.

All went according to plan on today's launch. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth as planned, touching down about 8.5 minutes after launch on the drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed in the Pacific Ocean. It was the 20th launch and landing for this particular booster, which is designated B1088.
The rocket's expendable upper stage, meanwhile, delivered the 27 spacecraft to LEO, deploying them there 62 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX announced via X.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

"Tomb Raider" celebrates its 30th anniversary this month. While many remember the iconic T-Rex or locking Winston the Butler in the freezer, many forget about the UFO in 1998’s "Tomb Raider III"; a mysterious alien craft that worked a lot like Doctor Who’s TARDIS.

Coming off the back of the hugely successful "Tomb Raider 2", developer Core Design had big plans for the third entry, including kayaking, those iconic London levels, and, of course, a level featuring a UFO in Area 51. Although it looked small on the outside, the UFO featured multiple floors for players to explore as they searched for a vital artifact, all as enemies swarmed in.

Now, I'm something of a Tomb Raider historian, and my upcoming book — "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" (available from October 30) — goes into detail about the making of "Tomb Raider III", "Tomb Raider IV", and other games in the series during those three years. While writing the book, I spoke to level designer Richard Morton about how the physics-defying UFO was made and how shows like "The X-Files" inspired him and the team.

When you start "Tomb Raider III", you find Lara in India, stumbling across one of four artifacts. After completing India, you can choose between London, South Pacific, and Nevada to collect the other artifacts before reaching the final section in Antarctica.

Richard Morton was one of the designers for "Tomb Raider III", who took on South Pacific and some of Nevada, a location that Neal Boyd had already begun work on before he moved to "Project Eden". Eventually, Lara would find herself in Area 51, with the final part of the level taking place in a UFO that houses the artifact she seeks.

“Area 51 was a bit of a team effort,” reveals Morton. “The part where the rocket launches, Neal did a lot of that stuff. So much of that level is his work, as well as some of the other routes. Andy Sandham helped in finishing off that level, too. And then the bit with the UFO, that was mine.”
Of course, a level called Area 51 needed aliens. In the late 1990s, UFOs were everywhere, ranging from TV shows like The X-Files to countless documentaries on whether aliens were real.

“We knew Area 51 had to have aliens in it in some form. And we did put some down on operating tables – we were all influenced by films and shows like 'The X-Files' and 'Independence Day', which were around at the time of TR3.”

You’d run past the UFO at certain points in between toggling switches, collecting keys, and even launching a rocket. Eventually, you’d unlock a door, letting you in to reveal an impossibly large interior. But all wasn’t as it seemed, and the journey to get here was fraught with challenges.

“I was working quite late one evening, and it wasn't a UFO to start with. I was working on the level and suddenly wondered what would happen if I had three rooms next to each other, with the room in the middle that was only the width of the portal,” explains Morton. “Then I’d link that to a separate room that was only visible inside the portal. I then somehow managed to build this impossible room that was surrounded by eight rooms – the only way I could get it to work. And it did, but it worked horizontally – it was just like Valve's 'Portal', but nine years before.”
AI programmer Tom Scutt, who had joined the team to improve the artificial intelligence for the enemies, worked with Morton to see how a portal could work in the level.

“Tom loved it, but I think he started doing some tests around it – this was just a portal in a room to see if it could be used. Soon after, he explained to me that enemies wouldn't work with it without being heavily reworked, because of how the navigation worked with the enemies,” Morton explains. “So if Lara went through a portal to 'another world', for example, the enemies wouldn't know; they'd just stay in the same room. So all in all, they basically said that they loved it, but you can't do it - and yet I kept trying.”

With Area 51 taking shape and the portal idea becoming viable, Morton realized that the two could become one, resulting in the UFO. “The next night, I decided to build a UFO, which we'd already built within the level in this rough shape in one of the hangars at the end of the level.”

That night, Morton cracked it, meaning the inside of the UFO could now be far bigger. “I built a ladder going up from the entrance, which went straight up through the tiny UFO model, which was only three by three blocks, with a one-block hole going up into it. So I remade the same trick from the night before, only vertically, and it worked!”
Still, despite getting the trick to work, more had to be done to ensure no bugs would emerge during this final section of the level.

“Once you got inside the UFO, I think we had to do a tiny bit of fiddling around, just to make the enemies warp inside the UFO. But they'd only try to attack you when you were in the UFO. I think we triggered them once you got in there and de-triggered them once you came out, just to stop them from firing at you when you weren't in there, just to keep that illusion of this TARDIS UFO going.”

Programmer Martin Gibbins, who had previously warned that the UFO would break everything, was won over by it. “Despite the UFO being Richard's idea, that was a testament to Gavin Rummery's ridiculous portal system. It had a single-block doorway into what was effectively a room. That was the clip window for the rest of the world, so you could do whatever you'd like inside of it. He got it working, and I thought it was great.”

For its time, it was an amazing feat on PlayStation and PC. With this being the third mainline "Tomb Raider" game, some players felt that the series was getting stale. But it was moments like the UFO and discovering it was far bigger than many initially thought that stuck with players, and still does to this day.

Unfortunately, another moment like the UFO would not happen in subsequent games, with the pressure of making the Thanksgiving deadline looming over the team. But Morton reveals that the team did speak about what could have alternatively happened at the end of the level.

"I think we talked about having a portal room that took you to another area that could have been either another location on Earth or another location across the galaxy. But obviously, we just didn't have time to do anything like that. It would have been awesome, though.”
However, after Morton spent two evenings trying to get the UFO to work and some on the team worried that it would break the game, it became a big highlight of "Tomb Raider III".

“When I showed the team the UFO, they were basically trembling, thinking, 'What have you done now!?' And we found out that it did work, and they ended up loving it. Looking back, I couldn't believe that I'd pulled it off, to be honest. I couldn't believe that the engine didn't just crash the game every time the camera looked into that portal. It didn't crash, and I thought, ‘Wow, that's awesome,’ at the time.”

The impossible geometry of the "Tomb Raider III" UFO is indeed an impressive spectacle, even almost 30 years later. If you’re interested in seeing how the TARDIS/UFO works, you can play "Tomb Raider III" via the Remastered collection, available on PlayStation 4/5, Xbox Series, Nintendo Switch 1/2, iOS, Android, and PC via Steam.
If you want to know more about "Tomb Raider 3" and its enigmatic UFO, "The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000" is available from October 30 via Pen and Sword, Amazon, and other retailers.

The Making of Tomb Raider: 1997-2000 tells the untold story of a pivotal period about one of the most successful video game series of all time, as a new development team at Core Design took charge of Tomb Raider in 1997.
Daryl is an entertainment writer and author of two books—The Making of Tomb Raider and 50 Years of Boss Fights.
Fire erupted in the morning skies over Siberia on June 30, 1908, as an atmospheric explosion occurred that remains unmatched by any similar event in modern history.

That day, at approximately 7:15 a.m. local time, observers in Siberia's remote Tunguska region became witnesses to the entry of a brilliant fireball into Earth's atmosphere, trailing smoke across the dawn sky and culminating in a flash brighter than the sun itself. Within seconds, the explosion and resulting shock waves that followed reportedly knocked some members of the nearby Indigenous Evenki population off their feet, and caused damage to dwellings and livestock, while seismic instruments hundreds of miles away logged tremors caused by the blast.

The blast produced enough energy to flatten a significant stretch of the Siberian wilderness, marking an event that still serves as a cautionary tale — and a major point of reference — for modern planetary defense efforts. Yet some questions remain about exactly what happened, and what the implications are for future potential Tunguska-scale events. For many years after the events of that day, the cause of the blast — known today as the Tunguska event — remained unknown. With time, a likely culprit emerged: scientists now believe a small asteroid, estimated to have been just 130 feet (40 meters) in diameter, exploded after entering Earth's atmosphere.

Remarkably, scientists wouldn't get a firsthand look at the destruction caused by the Tunguska blast for almost two decades, due primarily to the extreme remoteness of the blast location. Further complicating scientific investigations were the First World War, the Russian Revolution, and the ensuing civil war.

One of the earliest attempts to reach the blast site was initiated in 1921 by Soviet geologist Leonid Kulik, who failed in his first effort, but did eventually make his way to Tunguska six years later. Upon arriving, the devastation caused by the event was unmistakable even after nearly two decades.

Curiously, at the blast site's presumed epicenter, a small area of unaffected trees remained standing, albeit stripped of some of their bark and branches. The surrounding countryside, by comparison, was littered with large numbers of trees that were toppled as the shock waves produced by the exploding asteroid high above radiated downward.

In the decades that followed, additional assessment of the site that included expeditions and aerial surveys, primarily during the 1950s and 1960s, revealed another curious feature: a distinctive hourglass- or butterfly-shaped destruction zone spanning well over 800 square miles (2,070 square kilometers), with millions of trees estimated to have been flattened. Yet most curious of all had been what investigators did not find; despite a blast zone of this size, there was no evidence of an impact crater at Tunguska.

What the evidence seemed to suggest was that an explosion had occurred not on the surface following a massive impact, but instead high in Earth's atmosphere — probably as much as several miles above the Earth — as tremendous aerodynamic stresses caused the object to fragment and release its energy before reaching the ground.

A longstanding debate about the Tunguska object has centered on whether it was more likely an asteroid or a comet, although today, most evidence appears to favor an asteroid. Among the clues supporting an asteroid origin are mineral and chemical signatures identified in material collected from the region that researchers have argued are consistent with a stony or carbonaceous asteroid. However, identifying physical remnants definitively associated with the Tunguska object has remained challenging.

While the Tunguska event remains an enigma in some ways, it also offers modern researchers an opportunity to study one of the rare recent examples in Earth's geological history of a large-scale cosmic airburst.

Deeper in Earth's past — around 66 million years ago — a six-mile-wide (10 km) asteroid struck what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. The impact created the 120-mile-wide (190 km) Chicxulub crater in a cataclysmic event that drove mass extinctions across the planet, eliminating nearly three-quarters of the species that thrived on Earth until that time.

Of course, even objects orders of magnitude smaller than the object that created the Chicxulub crater can pose a danger to Earth. Although the object that struck Earth 66 million years ago is believed to have been as much as 200 times wider and millions of times more massive than the suspected asteroid that exploded over Siberia in 1908, estimates indicate that a Tunguska-scale event would be capable of killing millions if it occurred today over a city the size of New York.

Such estimates aren't based entirely on theory, either. In February 2013, planetary scientists were given a dramatic opportunity to gauge the effects of such an event when a previously undetected 60-foot-wide (20 meters) asteroid exploded after entering Earth's atmosphere over Chelyabinsk, Russia.

The resulting blast, which released energy equivalent to an estimated 500 kilotons of TNT, was captured on cameras throughout the region as it damaged buildings and caused injuries to more than 1,000 people, mostly due to flying glass from windows that were shattered by the blast wave.

Because of events like Chelyabinsk and Tunguska, planetary scientists have worked to expand initiatives that detect and monitor potentially hazardous near-Earth objects (NEOs) that could become a concern in the decades ahead.

Still, despite such efforts having been in effect at the time, the Chelyabinsk event represented an example of a potentially dangerous NEO that effectively managed to sneak up on us. Fortunately, despite the damage that was caused, things could have been far worse. But will we be so lucky next time?

To help mitigate such concerns, in 2016 NASA established the Planetary Defense Coordination Office to help align its efforts with those of its international partners and develop more advanced methods of identifying and tracking any NEOs that could pose an impact threat.

Then in 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated the use of a spacecraft as a kinetic impactor, which was intentionally sent on a collision course with Dimorphos, the small moon of the asteroid Didymos, which altered Dimorphos' orbital period around its companion by approximately 33 minutes. Such technology could one day prove to be vital if another potential Tunguska-type object were found to be on a collision course with Earth.
Fact, fiction, and planning for the future

Given the questions that remain about Tunguska, as well as the misrepresentations and persistent myths surrounding it, several scientists have also worked in recent years to combat misinformation about the 1908 event.

In a paper published in March 2026 in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science, authors Mark Boslough and colleagues noted that future planning for evacuation plans and other mitigation efforts "depend critically on our ability to model these events, which depends on our understanding of the governing physics, which in turn is validated by sparse data on real events such as Tunguska."
"If people do not have confidence in the models on which evacuation plans are based, they could lose their lives," the study's authors warned.

More than a century after it occurred, June 30 is now recognized as International Asteroid Day, commemorating not only the blast's anniversary, but also the need for awareness of the dangerous potential future similar events could present.

Tunguska therefore remains a source of fascination for scientists, as well as an opportunity to better understand — and to prepare for — any potential future threats posed by similar objects, should one eventually be found on a collision course with Earth.
Scientists discover why a 100-year-old mushroom disease won't go away

- Scientists have uncovered a surprising secret behind a mushroom disease that has frustrated growers for more than a century: It involves more than 17 species of harmful bacteria, not just one. The discovery could explain why treatments have struggled to stop the disease and open the door to more effective, eco-friendly solutions.

A disease that has troubled white button mushroom growers for more than 100 years is far more complicated than scientists previously believed. Researchers at the University of Florida have discovered that the problem involves a surprisingly diverse collection of harmful bacteria, rather than a single pathogen. The finding could help explain why the disease has been so difficult to control and lead to more effective ways to protect mushroom crops.
The discovery comes from a University of Florida study investigating bacterial blotch, a persistent disease that damages white button mushrooms and causes significant financial losses for growers.

White button mushrooms are a valuable specialty crop and a familiar ingredient in everything from salads and appetizers to everyday meals. Rich in nutrients and valued for their versatility, they are often promoted as an example of the "food is medicine" concept, which emphasizes the role of nutritious foods in supporting good health. Their nutritional benefits make them an important part of many healthy diets.
Despite their popularity, these mushrooms face a longstanding problem that can make entire portions of a harvest difficult or impossible to sell.
A Century-Old Mushroom Disease With Hidden Culprits

Bacterial blotch causes brown or yellow discoloration on mushroom surfaces, damaging their appearance and reducing their commercial value. The disease can also lower crop yields and shorten shelf life, making it a costly challenge for mushroom farms across the United States.

Adding to the difficulty, visible symptoms sometimes develop only after mushrooms have been shipped to grocery stores or purchased by consumers. This delayed appearance makes the disease especially troublesome for growers trying to ensure consistent product quality.

For many years, scientists primarily associated bacterial blotch with a single disease-causing bacterial pathogen. However, researchers at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) have now found that the disease involves a much more complex collection of pathogenic bacteria.

These microorganisms can thrive in the carefully controlled, humid indoor environments used for commercial mushroom cultivation. Because several bacterial species may contribute to the same disease, methods designed to target a single pathogen may not be sufficient.

"For years, the industry has struggled with treatments that provide inconsistent results against bacterial blotch," said Samuel Martins, co-author and assistant professor in the UF/IFAS Department of Plant Pathology. "As part of a separate $7 million U.S. Department of Agriculture grant involving Penn State, University of Delaware and UF/IFAS, we are developing advanced diagnostics and sustainable solutions to strengthen mushroom farms nationwide."
DNA Analysis Reveals More Than 17 Bacterial Species
To investigate what was causing the disease, the research team collected affected mushrooms from several production facilities across the southern United States.

The scientists combined DNA sequencing, chemical profiling and conventional laboratory testing to identify the bacteria associated with the damaged mushrooms. DNA sequencing allowed them to examine the genetic identities of microorganisms present in the samples, while the additional tests helped characterize the bacteria and their disease-causing potential.
The results revealed a far more diverse group of pathogens than expected.

"We found more than 17 different species of pathogenic bacteria associated with the disease," said Sameerika Mudiyanselage, the study's lead author and a doctoral student of Martins and Romina Gazis at UF/IFAS Tropical Research and Education Center. "While two well-known bacterial pathogens dominated the known disease profile, we also detected a surprisingly high level of another group of bacteria that has not previously been linked to the mushroom disease."

The discovery suggests that scientists have been overlooking important contributors to bacterial blotch. Although two established pathogens remained prominent, the presence of additional bacterial groups indicates that the disease cannot be fully understood by studying those organisms alone.

This complexity may help explain why bacterial blotch has persisted for generations despite efforts to manage it. When several different microorganisms are associated with a disease, identifying the responsible bacteria, predicting outbreaks, and developing consistently effective treatments become more challenging.
The findings also suggest that growers may need more comprehensive detection methods capable of identifying a broader range of bacterial threats.

"We hope that expanding our research will lead to the development of better diagnostics and more effective treatments to address the full group of disease-causing bacteria in white button mushrooms," she said.
Natural Treatments Could Help Protect Mushroom Farms
The University of Florida researchers are now building on their findings with a follow-up study focused on more sustainable ways to manage bacterial blotch.
One promising approach involves testing plant-based essential oils, beneficial microorganisms, and other biological products as possible alternatives to conventional chemical treatments.

Essential oils contain naturally occurring compounds produced by plants, some of which have antimicrobial properties. Beneficial microbes may also help suppress harmful bacteria or make it more difficult for disease-causing organisms to thrive.

These approaches could eventually offer mushroom growers additional tools for controlling bacterial blotch while reducing their reliance on conventional chemical treatments. However, further research is needed to determine how well the potential alternatives work under real growing conditions.

"Ultimately, our goal is to provide growers with practical, science-based solutions that help strengthen mushroom farming systems," said Martins. "By understanding the complexity of bacterial blotch and the role of microbial communities, we can develop better eco-friendly management practices that reduce losses while improving sustainability."

The research changes the understanding of a disease that has affected white button mushroom production for more than a century. Rather than being the work of a single bacterial pathogen, bacterial blotch involves a diverse group of potentially harmful microorganisms, including previously overlooked species.

By uncovering this hidden complexity, scientists hope to improve disease detection, develop more reliable treatments, and reduce the crop losses that have long burdened mushroom producers. The findings could ultimately help make mushroom farming more resilient, productive and environmentally sustainable.

The hidden math of Alzheimer's could point to new treatments

- Mathematics may hold unexpected clues to understanding Alzheimerâs disease. Scientists have developed a model showing how common metals like copper and zinc may influence the buildup of proteins associated with the disease, while also exploring possible ways to stop the process. The findings could help researchers identify promising strategies for preventing harmful plaque formation.

Could mathematics help uncover new ways to fight Alzheimer's disease? A researcher at Mississippi State University is using mathematical models to investigate how common metals influence the buildup of proteins associated with Alzheimer's and whether potential treatments could interfere with this process.

Shantia Yarahmadian, an associate professor in Mississippi State's Department of Mathematics and Statistics, is studying how metals such as copper and zinc may affect the behavior of amyloid-beta, a protein that can clump together and form plaques linked to Alzheimer's disease.

His research, published in the journal Bulletin of Mathematical Biology, builds on his ongoing efforts to use mathematics to better understand the complex biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
Using Mathematics To Understand Alzheimer's Disease

Mathematical modeling allows scientists to explore complicated biological interactions by representing them through equations and simulations. Researchers can then test how different factors influence a process and predict what might happen when certain conditions change.

"Every biological phenomenon occurs in the physical world -- in space and time -- and involves changes in shape, quantity and matter," said Yarahmadian, a faculty member in MSU's Department of Mathematics and Statistics. "Because of its abstract power, mathematics allows us to uncover patterns, test hypotheses and make predictions that may not be possible through observation alone. Mathematics does not replace laboratory or clinical research; it complements it by helping us understand the larger system, identify the most influential mechanisms and guide future experiments."
This approach could be particularly valuable for Alzheimer's disease, which involves numerous interacting biological processes that are difficult to study individually.
How Copper and Zinc May Influence Alzheimer's Plaques

To investigate how Alzheimer's-related plaques develop, Yarahmadian created a mathematical framework that simulates the chemical reactions involved when metals such as copper and zinc interact with amyloid-beta.

Amyloid-beta proteins can stick together in a process known as aggregation. Over time, these clusters can contribute to the formation of plaques, one of the characteristic features of Alzheimer's disease.

The model examines how metal ions, which are electrically charged forms of metals, may influence this protein buildup. It also enables researchers to explore two potential therapeutic approaches designed to interfere with aggregation.

Rather than relying entirely on laboratory experiments, scientists can use the simulations to investigate how changes in these interactions might affect plaque formation and identify promising directions for further research.
Mathematical Predictions Match Laboratory Results

A mathematical model is most useful when its predictions reflect what happens in actual experiments. To evaluate his framework, Yarahmadian and his collaborators compared its results with laboratory measurements obtained through atomic force microscopy.
This imaging technique uses an extremely fine probe to examine structures at the microscopic scale, allowing researchers to study tiny clusters of proteins and other materials.

The mathematical model successfully reproduced the patterns observed in the experiments. This agreement suggests that the framework captures important aspects of how amyloid-beta proteins aggregate under the conditions studied.

The results provide evidence that mathematical simulations can help researchers investigate the mechanisms behind protein clumping and explore ways to influence the process. Although the findings do not establish an effective Alzheimer's treatment, they offer a promising tool for guiding future laboratory studies.

For Yarahmadian, the motivation behind the research extends beyond the mathematical challenge. He hopes that a better understanding of the disease's complex biology will eventually help scientists develop more effective strategies against it.

"What drew me to Alzheimer's research is the combination of its profound human impact and its extraordinary biological complexity," he said. "My goal is to use mathematical modeling to identify important mechanisms and generate insights that may help guide future experimental and therapeutic research."

Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists

- Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life.

Imagine a universe where stars still shine, planets still form, and water exists, but liquids are so thick that living cells can barely function. Even with the chemical ingredients for life, the conditions might make living organisms impossible.

Scientists have uncovered a remarkable connection between the fundamental laws of physics and the ability of life to exist. Their findings suggest that even relatively small changes to some of the universe's most basic physical constants could dramatically alter how liquids flow, potentially preventing essential biological processes from taking place.

The discovery, detailed in a study published in Science Advances, came from physicist Kostya Trachenko at Queen Mary University of London. His theoretical analysis identified an additional constraint on the values of fundamental physical constants: They must permit liquids to move in ways that support life within and between cells.
The work raises a profound question about the universe. Why do the fundamental laws of nature have values that appear so well suited to the existence of life?
The Fundamental Constants That Shape Our Universe

Fundamental physical constants are numbers that govern how the universe operates. Examples include the mass and electric charge of an electron and the Planck constant, which plays a central role in quantum mechanics, the branch of physics that describes matter and energy at extremely small scales.

These quantities are generally considered universal and unchanging over time. Their values influence everything from the behavior of atoms and chemical bonds to the nuclear reactions that power stars and produce elements essential for life.
Despite their importance, scientists still do not know why these constants have the particular values we observe.
An important clue emerged in 2020, when Trachenko and his colleagues demonstrated that fundamental physical constants place a lower limit on the viscosity of liquids.

Viscosity describes how strongly a fluid resists flowing. Water has relatively low viscosity and pours easily, while honey and tar are much more viscous and move slowly. The researchers showed that there is a fundamental limit to how freely a fluid can flow, with that limit ultimately connected to the basic constants of nature.
The 2023 study took this connection much further by examining its implications for biology.
Why Tiny Changes to Physics Could Make Life Impossible

Every living cell depends on the movement of molecules. Nutrients must reach the places where they are needed, waste products must be transported away, and countless chemical reactions must occur in a liquid environment.

Another important process is diffusion, the natural spreading of particles through a fluid. Diffusion helps molecules move around cells and enables many of the chemical interactions required for life.

If the viscosity of those fluids changed too much, these processes could become severely disrupted. Liquids that were too thick might prevent vital materials from moving efficiently, while excessively low viscosity could also interfere with the controlled flow necessary for biological functions.
Trachenko explained the surprising connection:

"Understanding how water flows in a cup turns out to be closely related to the grand challenge to figure out fundamental constants. Life processes in and between living cells require motion and it is viscosity that sets the properties of this motion. If fundamental constants change, viscosity would change too impacting life as we know it. For example, if water was as viscous as tar life would not exist in its current form or not exist at all. This applies beyond water, so all life forms using the liquid state to function would be affected."

The implications extend beyond water. Although all known life depends on water, hypothetical organisms elsewhere in the universe might rely on different liquids. The same fundamental physical constraints would still influence how those liquids behave.
Trachenko suggested that the range of constants compatible with cellular life could be surprisingly narrow.

"Any change in fundamental constants including an increase or decrease would be equally bad news for flow and for liquid-based life. We expect the window to be quite narrow: for example, viscosity of our blood would become too thick or too thin for body functioning with only a few per cent change of some fundamental constants such as the Planck constant or electron charge."

These predictions come from theoretical models rather than experiments in which scientists actually changed fundamental constants. The precise limits that different forms of life could tolerate remain uncertain.
A Cosmic Mystery Billions of Years in the Making
What makes the findings especially intriguing is that the same fundamental constants that influence liquid flow also govern the nuclear reactions responsible for creating heavy elements inside stars.
Long before the first living cells appeared, stars were producing elements such as carbon and oxygen that would eventually become essential components of living organisms.

Physicists have long investigated whether the constants governing these nuclear processes must fall within certain ranges for complex matter to exist. But the ability to create life's chemical ingredients does not necessarily guarantee that life can function.
Trachenko's analysis showed that some physical properties governing liquid flow could change without disrupting the combinations of constants needed to produce heavy nuclei in stars.
In other words, a hypothetical universe might still produce the elements necessary for life while having liquids so viscous that cellular processes could not operate.

That means the conditions needed to support life may involve more than the ability to form stars, planets, and complex chemistry. The physical properties of liquids could impose additional requirements on the universe's fundamental constants.
Follow-Up Research Reveals a Surprising Connection to Blood
The investigation continued beyond the original discovery.

In a follow-up study published in January 2025 in The European Physical Journal E, Trachenko and colleagues examined how fundamental physical constants influence more complicated biological fluids, particularly blood.

Unlike water, blood is a complex mixture containing plasma, red blood cells, platelets, and other components. Its viscosity depends not only on molecular properties but also on how these components interact.

For example, red blood cells can form clusters that increase resistance to flow. As the blood moves faster, those clusters can break apart, allowing it to flow more easily. This behavior makes blood considerably more complicated than a simple liquid.

The researchers found something unexpected. Despite the enormous complexity of blood and the relatively large size of red blood cells, its viscosity remains surprisingly close, on a fundamental physical scale, to a theoretical value derived from basic physical constants.

They proposed that interactions between closely spaced blood cells may help explain this connection. Even though red blood cells are vastly larger than atoms, the forces acting where their surfaces approach one another involve distances small enough for molecular and quantum effects to matter.

The 2025 analysis also emphasized an important complication. Estimating which fundamental constants are compatible with life requires accounting for both the intrinsic properties of liquids, determined by fundamental physics, and the additional effects created by interactions among cells and molecules.
These findings offer a more detailed framework for investigating the connection between the universe's basic physical properties and the biological processes that depend on them.
The research also points toward an even deeper mystery: Why do the fundamental constants have values that allow so many different physical processes to work together?

One speculative possibility raised by Trachenko is that multiple forms of fine-tuning may be involved. The values that allow stars to manufacture heavy elements and those that permit liquids to support cellular life may represent separate requirements.
He suggested an intriguing analogy with biological evolution, in which different useful characteristics can emerge through separate processes.
Perhaps some broader evolutionary principle could help explain how nature arrives at combinations of physical properties capable of supporting stable structures and increasingly complex systems.

For now, this remains a conjecture. Scientists have not established that fundamental constants evolve through such a mechanism, nor have they determined why those constants possess their observed values.
Still, the connection between liquid flow and fundamental physics opens another way to investigate one of science's biggest unanswered questions.
Something as ordinary as water moving through a glass, or blood circulating through the body, may hold clues to why the universe has the physical properties that make life possible.

Sometimes we receive strange, ghostly radio signals from outer space, which astronomers have yet to conclusively explain.
Partially because they disappear almost as soon as they arrive.
The ephemera known as fast radio bursts (FRBs) are among the Universe's most mysterious occurrences, even more eerie than the supposed little green aliens with a penchant for physical probes.
If they were related, that would neatly solve two major mysteries.
But FRBs are bursts of radio waves from the distant cosmos, generally lasting for tiny fractions of a second (i.e., fast).
Their transience, and the fact that they randomly appear across the sky, have made it difficult to pin down their origins for nearly two decades since their discovery in 2007.

But we just got a huge clue: Astronomers have reported the most distant FRB yet, designated FRB 20240304B, a burst of ancient energy that was emitted in one-thousandth of a second and has traveled through 80 percent of the Universe's history to meet us.
"What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them," explains lead author Manisha Caleb, a radio astronomer and astrophysicist at the University of Sydney.
"We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof."

So, who's the cosmic culprit in this specific case? Possibly a magnetar: a type of neutron star on steroids that packs the most powerful magnetic fields in the Universe and squeezes the mass of a whole Sun into a magnetic marble the size of San Francisco Bay.

Yet here's another conundrum: despite their incomprehensibly intense origins, and their ability to release 500 million Suns' worth of energy in thousandths of a second, they may be light(er)weights compared to other stellar outbursts, which has led to a sampler platter of possibilities and added to the difficulty of their conclusive identification:
"We observationalists can only kill models, never prove them. So, when you have 100 to kill, it takes a fair bit of time." – astronomer and astrophysicist J. Xavier Prochaska

"Fundamentally, it is because the energies involved are modest. They are extreme for radio wave emission, but nothing like the energy in a supernova or gamma-ray burst," J. Xavier Prochaska, an astronomer and astrophysicist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told ScienceAlert.
"As such, theorists have devised nearly 100 models to generate them.
"We observationalists can only kill models, never prove them. So, when you have 100 to kill, it takes a fair bit of time."

In the study, published in the journal Science, a massive, international collaboration of astronomers used multiple observatories to explore this mysterious FRB emanating from 'cosmic noon,' an era only 3 billion years after the Big Bang when Universal star formation was at its peak.
The astronomers identified the FRB in March 2024 using MeerKAT, a 64-antenna radio telescope in South Africa's Meerkat National Park.
They then pointed two ultra-sensitive ground telescopes at the corresponding patch of sky to see its host galaxy and discovered… darkness.
They looked as deep as they could "but there was simply nothing to see," Prochaska says.
So they called in the heavy orbital artillery (just a metaphor, for now), the JWST and its exceptional infrared sensitivity.
And if the researchers suspected a monster, they found a mouse:
"We thought it would be a big, nicely formed galaxy with lots of stars, and instead it was a little dwarf galaxy, although it was actively forming stars," says Caleb.
Altogether, this dwarf galaxy is 1,000 times less massive than expected.
It's also exceedingly young, with 90 percent of its stellar mass having formed in the past 30 million years.
This helped the astronomers favor a magnetar as the potential source of the historic FRB.
Another prominent FRB scenario involves the collision of two neutron stars, a cataclysmic crash that yields a black hole or an extra-heavy neutron star, plus a bunch of literal gold.
Yet neutron stars dance around each other for billions of years before colliding, like a still-shy couple on a second date, so it wouldn't make sense in a young galaxy.
Magnetars, however, can form and release their magnetic energy in just millions of years. Especially in a metal-poor galaxy like this that breeds massive stars.
Also, like good guests, FRBs come bearing gifts of the astrophysical kind.
Even though light travels at the speed of itself, the ultimate breakneck physical limit, it only does so in a vacuum.
And as this FRB passed through the cold, ionized (electrically charged) gas that permeates the cosmos, its lower-frequency waves were slowed more than its higher ones, so they arrived later.
Turbulent gas, most likely in its home galaxy, also scattered the signal, smearing it out over several milliseconds
FRBs thus act as an astronomical flashlight, and this particular one has had its signal warped by two cosmic-scale structures as it traversed most of the Universe to meet us.

In doing so, it helped illuminate an unknown galaxy group along the way, located about 3.5 billion light-years away, while also bearing the ionic imprint of the Virgo Cluster, the nearest such structure to Earth, only around 54 million light-years distant.

Finally, since we only know of about 100 FRBs whose host galaxies have been confirmed, the researchers note, and most are billions of light-years more local, this wasn't just the cherry atop the celestial sundae, but a whole other sundae on top of the sundae.
"Because we have scant understanding of what generates FRBs, we could only hope that they might exist at such early times," Prochaska told ScienceAlert.
"Now, we have proven it and this will drive new, dedicated studies to find others – and search even greater distances!"
Sound can be a tricksy beast to try to harness.

It fills the world around us, bursting from its multitudinous sources, bouncing off surfaces as echoes – a property that makes sound both incredibly useful and deeply vexing, depending on where and how its reverberations occur.

There are some circumstances where echoes can cause problems. The most obvious example is sound recording studios, but one major problem area is probably less obvious because it's far more ubiquitous – pipes.

Consider ventilation, air conditioning, industrial exhaust, or even plumbing. Sound travels through the spaces enclosed in those pipes and ducts, and when it encounters an obstruction, a change in shape, or a closed end, it can start to rattle around like nobody's business.
Now, scientists have developed an ingenious little device that can dramatically reduce those reflections by effectively 'swallowing' sound.

It's called a sonic black hole, and the new design can be 3D-printed and inserted directly into an existing pipe – a major step forward from conventional designs that require the black hole to be built into the pipe itself.

"Imagine standing in front of a duct that is closed at the far end and shouting into it. After a short delay, depending on the length of the duct, you would hear an echo coming back from the termination," acoustics engineer Oriol Guasch of La Salle, Universitat Ramon Llull in Spain told ScienceAlert.

"If the duct were terminated with a sonic black hole, you would essentially hear no echo at all. Acoustically, it would be almost as if the tube were infinitely long, with no end from which the sound could be reflected back towards you."
Black holes are best known as astrophysical objects, pockets of space so dense that their gravity warps the space-time around them into a spherical horizon from which not even light can escape.

There are many reasons why we can't study these objects up close, so physicists have devised other methods, creating laboratory analogs that reproduce aspects of black hole behavior, sometimes relying on phenomena that have little to do with gravity.

But the 'black hole' developed by Guasch and colleagues, described in a paper first authored by engineer Jie Deng of La Salle, Universitat Ramon Llull, is a different kind of beast inspired by what a black hole can do.

Rather than using sound to simulate gravitational physics, it's designed to exploit an unusual property of sound waves: under the right conditions, they can be progressively slowed until they effectively never reach the end of their journey.

It's a little like the ancient Greek philosopher Zeno's famous dichotomy paradox, in which a traveler must cover half the remaining distance to a destination, then half again, and so on, seemingly never arriving.
The difference is that, in a sonic black hole, the wave really does slow down as it travels.

"What happens to the wave as it approaches the end of a sonic black hole has a certain resemblance to what the external observer sees near an astrophysical black hole: the wave appears to take an infinite time to reach the limiting point," Guasch explained.
"In the ideal case, once a wave enters the sonic black hole, it does not come back out."

The acoustic vanishing trick lies in the design. Just as an astrophysical black hole is not actually a hole, neither is the sonic version. It's a carefully engineered structure that changes the way sound travels through a pipe.

In conventional designs, a series of rings and cavities line the inside of the pipe, arranged so that sound waves slow down progressively as they travel through it. Their wavelengths become shorter, and their energy becomes increasingly concentrated.

But there's a catch. These structures have to be built into the pipes themselves, usually manufactured together, making them difficult to retrofit into existing systems. And the black-hole effect only works across a limited range of sound frequencies.
Deng, Guasch, and their colleagues wondered whether they could solve both problems by turning the whole thing inside out – a sonic Christmas tree, rather than a funnel.

"The concept is surprisingly simple, and it works very well," Guasch said. "From a practical point of view, the sonic black hole can be manufactured independently of the duct and then simply inserted into it."

The team's design consists of a series of rings mounted on a central rod, with their diameters gradually changing along its length. The spaces between the rings form cavities that mess with the way sound travels through the pipe.
As sound enters the structure at the tip, it slows down, its wavelength becoming progressively shorter as its energy concentrates towards the far end.

And here's where that vanishing trick happens. Rather than simply bouncing back, much of the concentrated sound energy is dissipated through friction and heat exchange between the air and the device's surfaces, leaving far less to escape as an echo.

The researchers tested this with a 3D-printed prototype – a 15-centimeter-long structure consisting of 29 rings mounted on a central rod, which was then inserted into an impedance tube – a laboratory apparatus used to measure how sound waves behave when they encounter a material or structure.
Then they yelled into the tube – not really; they used a speaker to send sound waves at different frequencies through the tube and microphones to measure how much bounced back.

And the results were pretty promising. The amount of sound reflected back out of the sonic black hole broadly matched the team's computer simulations – although it's important to note that it didn't completely eliminate echoes.
The researchers also used computer simulations to compare their plug-in design with a conventional sonic black hole.
These suggested that the new geometry could have benefits that go beyond modularity and ease of installation.
"The other important advantage is that the frequency range over which the device behaves as a sonic black hole is considerably wider than in the conventional configuration," Guasch explained.
The simulations also showed that the plug-in design reflected less sound than its conventional counterpart across a broad range of frequencies.
This is because the cavities between the rings in a sonic black hole resonate at particular sound frequencies, changing the way the device absorbs sound.
In the new design, the researchers found that those resonances occur at higher frequencies, allowing the black-hole effect to keep working over a broader range.
The most immediate applications for this technology are, obviously, in noise control, particularly in ducts and silencers where reflected sound can cause problems.
And the researchers are already looking beyond pipes, investigating whether sonic black holes could be developed in two and three dimensions, with potential applications in room acoustics.
Related: Physicists Simulated a Black Hole in a Lab. Then It Started to 'Evaporate'.

There are still challenges to overcome before the little sound-devouring Christmas trees can be deployed in the wild. Different environments bring different problems, from particles that could clog the cavities to the effects of temperature, pressure, and flowing air.
But Guasch is excited by the possibilities of manipulating sound in ways that would once have seemed almost impossible.

"Personally, what I find most stimulating is the physics and mathematics behind all of this, and the way it brings together areas of knowledge that may initially seem quite unrelated," he told ScienceAlert.
"And, of course, the type of wave control that can now be achieved would probably have seemed almost like science fiction several years ago."
The research has been published in Applied Acoustics.

BANGKOK – The International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, as rising inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowings pressure sovereign bond markets.

Government bond yields in several advanced economies have climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs due to the Middle East conflict and expectations for tighter monetary conditions as central banks look to curb resurgent inflation.

In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, the fund warned that sovereign bond risk could deteriorate, warning of "a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields." The report was released Tuesday as part of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, this week, where more than 18,000 delegates gathered to discuss the state of the world economy and the financial system.

High debt load and rollover risks make the bond market "susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks," the report said. The IMF had warned last week that global public debt had reached near its highest level since World War II and was on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP.

"Impact could be severe given the foundational importance of sovereign bond markets," the IMF said Tuesday. A sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values through higher discount rates, including for AI-related assets, and erode the value of government bonds posted as collateral.

IMF also noted the exponentially rising borrowing by AI firms — that compete with sovereign bonds for investor demand — as an additional source of strain on bond markets. Hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade bond issuance has risen to 10% from less than 1% since 2024, the report said.
The global AI buildout has seen tech giants, such as Alphabet Inc's Google, Meta Platforms, hyperscalers and AI labs raising hundreds of billions of dollars in debt this year.

"AI-linked issuance – much of it longer-dated – has grown large enough to compete with government bonds for investor capital, even if it does not appear to be the dominant driver of yields," according to Marc Seidner, CIO of non-traditional strategies at Pacific Investment Management.
On the bright side, liquidity measures remain stable in the U.S., Europe and the U.K., the IMF said, and market functioning "has been orderly."

While hedge funds' leveraged Treasury basis trades have partly unwound without notable pressure in repurchase markets, the leverage that remains leaves the market "susceptible to a disorderly unwind," according to the report.
Hedge funds' share of U.S. Treasuries rose to about 9% in 2025 from about 4% in 2022, mostly through highly arbitraged strategies, the IMF said, citing data from the Federal Reserve.
Japan is the exception on liquidity, which has "continued to deteriorate" in its government bond market as yield volatility has risen since the end of yield curve control, the IMF said.
The fund urged debt managers to lengthen maturities, warning that rollover risk could be exacerbated by strategies that replace long-term debt with short-term borrowing on a large scale.

Danny Boyle and his starry cast, led by Jack O’Connell and Guy Pearce, took to the BFI London Film Festival carpet for the U.K. premiere on Monday night, around a month after it opened the Venice Film Festival.

“I expect the difference to be palpable,” began O’Connell, star of Sinners and 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple, to The Hollywood Reporter about finally putting Ink in front of its native audience. “It’s a London film. If it doesn’t work here, it’s not going to work anywhere.”

The movie, adapted from James Graham’s stage play, depicts Pearce’s Rupert Murdoch as he enters the British newspaper scene, acquiring the then-failing tabloid The Sun in 1969. Hiring Larry Lamb (O’Connell) as editor, the two combined far-right political reporting and populist rabble to turn the paper into a dark force in British media. Murdoch would take the lessons learned at The Sun and apply them to build his U.S. media empire with The New York Post and Fox News.

Backdropped by the smoky, seedy journalistic epicentre that is Fleet Street, O’Connell said he didn’t categorize the notorious Lamb as a “bad” person. “I think he was just perhaps overly ambitious,” said the star. “I think this guy was on a pursuit, or his obsession was newspapers, and I guess he broke a couple of rules along the way. And it wasn’t victimless, but yeah, I don’t consider him an out-and-out bad guy.”

Pearce, on the other hand, told THR he’s keen to meet up with Murdoch for brunch. He said about being cast as the Australian-born media mogul: “Liz [Murdoch] told me that her dad was happy with me playing him, but I don’t know to what degree that is. I can’t really speak to that, to be honest. He might watch the film and go, ‘Eugh! Jesus Christ, what were they thinking?'” He certainly thinks that the feature “will resonate” with fans in the British capital.

Boyle, director of Trainspotting, Slumdog Millionaire and 28 Days Later, said the film showcases an integral origin story that speaks to the sensationalism of our current climate. “You can argue about whether they introduced this entirely or whether they nurtured something that was latent within us,” he said to THR. “But it is the beginnings of the attention economy, of the clickbait economy, of the ‘What’s next? Swipe, move on.’ It’s the very beginnings of it there, the beginnings of the fire, and now it’s a bushfire that’s all around us, everywhere. And I don’t know whether we’re going to survive it… But if you want to understand it, I think there’s a very good case for this [as] the place where it began.”

Playwright Graham concurred with Boyle’s analysis, explaining that Ink is a deeply British piece of work. “I really believe that by drilling down into its Englishness and the ’60s, the people in America, Europe, everywhere will relate to this story, which is essentially a story about how a disruptive bunch of people in the ’60s turned something around,” he said. “[The Sun] was the worst-selling paper in England and [they] made it the biggest-selling paper in the world, and I feel like people will link that to what’s happening at the moment in tech and Silicon Valley and that culture of breaking things, disrupting things, challenging things.” (Boyle actually likened Lamb and Murdoch’s achievement of out-selling The Daily Mirror to “a local pub team beating Real Madrid.”)

The screenwriter continued about the unique beast that is Fleet Street: “No other country in the world has had its newspapers on one street with all the restaurants and bars and culture, and I feel like the richness of that and the seduction of that, but also the ugliness of that specificity, really appeals to people across the world.”

British star O’Connell, who has also collaborated with Boyle on the 28 Years Later films, jokingly said the director’s “gone quiet” about their next project together, though admitted they are “inseparable.” On which film from this year he’d have liked to have been involved in, the actor coyly confessed it’d be Martin McDonagh’s CIA tragicomedy Wild Horse Nine.

The 70th BFI London Film Festival runs Oct. 7-18, and opened with the European premiere of Andrew Scott’s tearjerker Elsinore. Some of the glitziest galas so far include Wild Horse Nine, Artificial, Paper Tiger, Possible Love, Bunker and La Bola Negra. BEIRUT, Lebanon, Oct. 12 (UPI) -- The European Union decided Monday to establish a new support mission to advise and strengthen the Lebanese Army and internal security forces for an initial period of three years.
EU Foreign Affaires Ministers agreed to launch a new European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, during a meeting in Brussels, according to an EU statement.

Kaja Kallas, high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, said the mission will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to "strengthen territorial control, border security and internal security."

"Europe is invested in Lebanon's future," Kallas said, adding that with this new mission, the EU continues to support the country's institutions in "restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people."
According to the Council of the EU, the mission will have an initial three-year mandate and comprise military and civilian pillars.

The military pillar will provide advisory support and training to strengthen the Lebanese Army's capabilities in "border security and maritime security," including intelligence, surveillance and counter-smuggling.

The civilian pillar will support the Internal Security Forces through "advisory support and specialized training" in areas such as cybercrime and anti-smuggling, as well as efforts to strengthen port security governance, including at the Port of Beirut.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the EU's decision to support the country's military and security institutions, saying it reflects "Europe's firm commitment to Lebanon's security and stability."

In a statement, Aoun said the EU's new mission would help strengthen the capabilities of Lebanon's legitimate institutions, extend the state's authority across its entire territory, and secure its borders, in line with the government's decisions on restricting weapons to legitimate security forces.

The EU decision comes as Lebanon seeks to strengthen state control over its territory and disarm Hezbollah, while the mandate of the United Nations peacekeeping force in southern Lebanon, or UNIIFIL, is to expire at the end of this year.

Chuck Hoskin Jr. fondly recalls watching a room full of Cherokee immersion students crowd around a screen to watch How to Train Your Dragon. Except Hiccup and Astrid weren't speaking English—the protagonists were speaking Cherokee, dubbed by voices from the local community.

“They're hearing it in our mother tongue—that didn't happen a generation ago,” Hoskin Jr., principal chief of the Cherokee Nation, tells WIRED. “We're a long way, thankfully, from rote classroom instruction and memorization to a world where kids can see the sort of creativity that sparks imagination and helps every kid become more articulate and literate.”

The Cherokee Nation has around 1,500 active speakers left, and most are over 70. Hoskin Jr. says the community is rapidly losing that generation, which is why it has spent time training up second-language learners. It even has a baby immersion program, hoping their first words are Cherokee.

“The foes we’ve had historically are the so-called Age of Discovery, colonization, the displacement of our people economically and geographically, boarding schools,” he says. “But it's nothing compared to the mathematics we’re up against now. Which is why we’re filled with this urgency every day to do all we can to find partners that can help us accelerate what we want to do.”

One of those accelerants is Apple. The Cherokee Nation has long collaborated with the iPhone maker, and Cherokee was the first Native American language included in iOS in 2010. Today, Apple says its iOS keyboard supports more than 200 languages and language variants, with a handful added last year in iOS 26, like Haitian Creole and Nez Perce. In iOS 27, it expanded support for Indigenous languages to include other Native American languages like Blackfoot, Comanche, and Northern East Cree.

The goal is to meet young people where they already spend much of their waking hours: phone screens. Hoskin Jr. says that to revitalize and save a language, it has to become accessible. Apple says the effort isn't as simple as translating words. It’s a multi-year endeavor that requires deep research, and the company leans on community members for their expertise.

But the process doesn’t start in Cupertino. It actually begins with Unicode. You may have heard of the name—it’s the organization that approves and standardizes the new emoji that appear on your smartphone every year. It also handles time zone localization, currency names, imperial versus metric, and so on.

Before you can type or read a character on a smartphone screen, it needs to exist as a recognized character in the Unicode Standard. “Everything does start with Unicode in terms of a language, but it actually starts with characters and scripts,” says Unicode CEO Toral Cowieson. “We now have more than 157,000 characters that are included.”

Cowieson calls Unicode a kind of digital Switzerland—a neutral consortium where rivals like Apple, Microsoft, and Google sit at the same table as linguists and volunteer contributors. (Cowieson told WIRED earlier this year that Unicode had only four full-time employees.) Proposing a language, verifying it, and then encoding the character set can take three to five years.

After a script is encoded, platforms like Apple and Google need to add font support. Without this step, a character could appear as an empty box—often called “tofu.” Next is orthography: a set of rules and systems for writing a language. Often, languages have a well-defined orthography, but when it’s not standardized, communities use ad hoc replacements because historically available keyboards don't support it.

Take the glottal stop—the speech sound made in the throat between the syllables when you say, “uh-oh.” Some languages have distinct characters for glottal stops, but as some keyboards don’t support them, many indigenous cultures use alternatives, like a question mark, to represent the sound. That's when Apple connects with the community to figure out the best way to represent the sounds in digital text.

That brings us to the keyboard layout. When a community already has an established physical keyboard layout—like Osage—Apple adapts it directly to the software keyboard. Some cultures prefer the QWERTY layouts people are already familiar with.

Other languages need more custom approaches. For example, Nez Perce, or Nimipuutímt, does not use capital letters. Rather than having the Shift key toggle traditional uppercase letters, Apple repurposed it to reveal an accented secondary layer, so users don’t have to hold down individual keys to see those characters, which can slow typing. In the Cherokee language, each character mostly represents a consonant combined with a vowel sound, a form known as syllabary. Apple added adaptive vowel keys on the bottom row, so when a user types a consonant, these keys change to show the vowel combinations they can make.
That’s a newer change to the Cherokee keyboard—one Apple approached the community about, meaning building a keyboard for a language isn’t a one-and-done project.

But digitizing an indigenous culture’s language hasn't always been harmless. Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Maya scholar and researcher at Bishop's University, studies how Indigenous people use digital technologies to reclaim language heritage. He recalls how Māori speakers rejected proposals to sell their language to tech companies.

“There’s a historical memory about the ways of dispossession that Indigenous peoples have experienced in the world,” Llanes-Ortiz says. “Māori working in their own revitalization efforts have been very firm in protecting access and storage of their linguistic materials because they have been exploited. They have experienced extraction of knowledge in the past.”

Language sovereignty and data ownership are top of mind, according to Chirasree Mandal, an Apple software engineer. “We don’t own anything, and we make it very clear that we are not trying to silo any data that we gain from this process,” she says. “It’s about making sure that the best choice for representing someone’s language is being made on our platform so they feel good using it.”

For its part, a Google spokesperson tells WIRED it has a long history of bringing lesser-known and Indigenous languages to its platforms so people can communicate, pointing to collaborations to integrate languages like Manx and Māori. Google also says it’s exploring how generative AI can simplify the coding and research required for new languages, but “successful integrations require direct participation from native speakers” for the keyboard to meet the community’s needs.

Hoskin Jr. says that writing in syllabary is seen as a badge of honor for young Cherokee speakers. People type their names in Cherokee on Facebook—that’s empowering. But he sees that progress as vulnerable to broader political rhetoric in the US that pushes a monolithic, English-speaking America, which he says bypasses several chapters, including Native American history.

“The greatest enemy we have right now for saving the Cherokee language is the passage of time and the fragility of human life,” Hoskin Jr. says. “Time is precious to everyone, but particularly precious to us in this mission.”

US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.

The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.

Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”

Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.

The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.

Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.

The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.

“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.
Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.

The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.

The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.

The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.

DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.

The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.
While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.

A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record

Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.
In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”

The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.

The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.
