Ever drive a vehicle that just doesn’t feel right anymore? Maybe it wanders down the highway. Maybe there’s a clunk every time you hit a pothole. Maybe the steering wheel isn’t centered, the tires are wearing unevenly, or it just doesn’t inspire the confidence it used to.

The truth is, steering and suspension problems rarely come from a single worn out part. Every control arm, ball joint, tie rod, sway bar link, and bushing work together as one connected system. When one connection starts to wear, it puts added stress on the rest of the system, and before long, that small problem becomes several bigger ones.
That system level approach is exactly how TrakMotive has positioned its Suspensia brand chassis program. Learn more about it in this video, sponsored by TrakMotive.

Super Cruise is GM’s hands-free driver-assistance system, offered on certain 2019-205 GM vehicles. Feature-wise, it combines adaptive cruise control, automatic braking, lane centering, driver monitoring, GPS and high-definition map data.

In the shop, diagnosis starts by separating a component fault or configuration problem from a normal system inhibit. A missing condition or failure in any of the above-mentioned areas can prevent engagement.

On an approved mapped road, Super Cruise uses Adaptive Cruise Control to manage speed and following distance while the lane-control system commands electric power steering to center the vehicle. The forward camera supplies lane information, and Adaptive Cruise Control sensing hardware tracks traffic ahead. The engine and electronic brake control modules carry out acceleration and braking requests. Because these modules exchange network data, a voltage, communication or configuration fault outside the camera can disable the system.

Super Cruise also compares GPS position with its map database. GM service information identifies the K179 Automated Driving Mapping Module and a LiDAR-scanned map database. Map and GPS-enhancement updates are downloaded through the vehicle’s OnStar Wi-Fi connection. The K73 telematics module supplies GPS and connectivity functions. If the vehicle cannot establish its location or does not have usable road data, Super Cruise cannot confirm that the road is eligible.

Before condemning hardware, verify the enabling conditions. Adaptive Cruise Control must be on, the Forward Collision System set to Alert and Brake, the road approved in the map database, lane markings visible, sensors unobstructed and the driver attentive. Teen Driver mode cannot be active. An OnStar plan and accepted terms may also be required. Requirements vary by model year and RPO, so identify the vehicle configuration before testing.

The secondary DIC message is often more useful than the general statement that Super Cruise is unavailable. “No Road Information” may indicate an ineligible road, an interchange, reconstruction, missing map data or lost GPS. The message “Sensors Can’t Find Lane Lines” can result from weak markings, glare or precipitation. “Sensor Blocked” points toward contamination. Other normal inhibits include an exit lane, a sharp curve, failure to center the vehicle or excessive speed. The referenced GM application lists 85 MPH, although limits are calibration-dependent.

“Could Not Recognize Face,” “Can’t See Face Clearly,” “Driver Attention Assist Unavailable,” momentary engagement followed by a takeover warning, and unexplained disengagement can originate in the monitoring system. Check for glare, a dirty lens, obstructions, steering-column position, a hand covering the infrared emitters, a loose B292 camera in the upper shroud, wiring damage or failed emitters. These complaints may occur without a DTC.

First, record the exact messages the customer received, along with road and location, weather, lighting, speed, engagement time and repeatability. Ask them about recent windshield, collision, steering, alignment, suspension, camera, radar or module work. Verify the OnStar account and terms when applicable, plus Wi-Fi and map-update status.

Next, perform GM’s vehicle diagnostic system check. Confirm battery state of charge, 9-16 V operating voltage where specified, clean and tight cables and grounds, intact fuses, seated connectors, correct power modes and the absence of interfering aftermarket equipment. Inspect lenses, radar areas and the steering-column camera before connecting the scan tool.

Run a full vehicle DTC scan and document every non-communicating module, DTC, symptom byte and current or history status. Do not erase evidence first. Diagnose voltage, internal-module, communication, power-mode and serial-data authentication faults before the Super Cruise symptom. Check applicable bulletins and calibrations. On covered 2021-2024 vehicles, intermittent startup U1624 in K124 may be a false loss-of-Ethernet fault caused by K73 telematics software; follow the bulletin and update K73. For other programmable modules, GM directs current software and a retest before replacement. Cruise data can retain the last eight disengagement reasons and the most recent engagement inhibit.

For “No Road Information” without a related DTC, move the vehicle to an open-sky area and inspect the K73 telematics data, including Number of Satellites Tracked when available. A value that remains at zero, or an incorrect location during an OnStar blue-button check, supports a GPS or telematics fault on vehicles covered by the applicable bulletin. Separate that failure from temporary map, road or reception limits.

For low-light face-recognition complaints, verify all three infrared emitters on each side of the steering-wheel light bar. GDS2 can command them through K124 Image Processing Module 1 Processor 2 under Configuration Reset Functions and Driver Monitoring System Illumination Command. GM recommends a phone camera with a long-exposure function because infrared output may be difficult to see. If one side is dark, follow the VIN-specific circuit diagnostics.

Programming, setup and calibration requirements differ across the 2019-2025 range. Confirm RPO content and follow the exact SI procedure after related components are replaced or disturbed. Some 2022-2023 vehicles with RPO 07Z use an image-processing module only to complete CAN circuits. Installing a functional replacement can create a “Take Steering Wheel” message unless the published configuration procedure is followed.

Complete all required programming, setup and calibrations, then clear the codes only as directed. Road-test the vehicle safely on a known compatible route and reproduce the original conditions. Confirm that the enabling indicators appear, the original DIC message does not return, driver monitoring responds and no faults reset. A successful bay check does not prove the complaint is resolved by itself.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) plans to modernize its outdated vehicle lighting standards, saying doing so will make America’s roads safer for all drivers, according to a press release.

NHTSA says an update to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 108 is “long overdue,” and that it will accelerate the rulemaking process by consulting with industry stakeholders, safety advocates, and technical experts.
The release states the discussions will cover key safety and engineering challenges, including:
- “Addressing headlight glare: Examining the role that modern headlighting technology has on glare for other road users and making appropriate changes.
- “Modernizing lighting technology: Improving rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams, and replaceable light sources.
- “Improving performance: Evaluating how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility.
- “Updating testing and materials: Streamlining test procedures for plastic optics and replaceable lenses.
- “Aligning global standards: Harmonizing U.S. vehicle lighting regulations with international safety standards.”
The release notes that this is the first time in more than 25 years that NHTSA is using negotiated rulemaking to update its vehicle lighting standards.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy plans to appoint up to 18 stakeholders across vehicle lighting manufacturers, motor vehicle equipment associations, safety organizations, research institutions, and engineering associations.
According to NHTSA’s rulemaking notice, it proposes the following representation:
- “Four representatives from vehicle lighting manufacturers or lighting retailers;
- “Two representatives from national motor vehicle manufacturers;
- “Four representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment manufacturing associations;
- “Two representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment safety organizations;
- “Three representatives from educational institutions or research institutions, or testing organizations within the United States; and
- “Three representatives from national professional engineering associations or standard-setting associations.”
The notice states that the committee will be “tasked with developing a detailed term sheet consisting of consensus recommendations to inform the agency’s rulemaking proposal.”
“NHTSA has long recognized the complexity of FMVSS No. 108 and the need to modernize the standard to facilitate new vehicle designs and emerging technologies,” the notice states.

It notes that NHTSA initiated rulemaking action RIN 2127-AL95 in the Spring 2018 Unified Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions. The notice states that the ongoing effort led to a rulemaking petition from Osram Sylvania regarding LED replacement light sources.

“Given the technical challenges of updating these legacy requirements, NHTSA recognizes that the expertise of outside stakeholders is essential in any highly technical discussion of revising FMVSS No. 108,” the notice states.

“The effort will cover various topics of modernization, such as glare caused by headlighting systems, replaceable light sources, dusk sensors, plastic optical materials, semiautomatic beam switching, minimum lamp size requirements, lower beam photometry, upper beam photometry, on-vehicle headlamps performance that considers aim and mounting height, auxiliary lamp requirements, three-wheel motorcycle installation requirements, obsolete physical test requirements for associated equipment, physical test procedures for lamps that use replaceable lenses, and harmonization to international standards.”
NHTSA says an abstract published in the Unified Agenda for RIN 2127-AL95 includes some of the topics.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison in the release. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”

NHTSA has asked for public comments on the rulemaking scope and committee membership. It also requests formal membership nominations. The deadline for comments and membership applications is Nov. 9. Both can be submitted here under Docket No. NHTSA-2026-1981.
In 2022, NHTSA issued a final rule allowing OEMs to install adaptive driving beam (ADB) headlights on new vehicles to increase visibility and reduce headlight glare.

NHTSA ruled that ADBs would improve safety for pedestrians and bicyclists by making them more visible at night and would help prevent crashes by better illuminating animals and objects in and along the road, according to the final rule. However, NHTSA states in the rule that “glare dosage,” or the amount of glare, “has not established, and does not know of, a quantified relationship between glare dosage and crash risk.”

Toyota has opened a new battery center in Saline, Michigan, calling it “the next chapter of its electrification transformation.”

On site, teams of engineers and technicians assess battery performance and develop new technologies for use in hybrid, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen, and fully electric vehicles.

Toyota says the 30,000-square-foot facility serves as a central hub for development and evaluation, in partnership with Toyota’s North American manufacturing network, to support battery evaluation for Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina, as well as the OEM’s vehicle manufacturing plants across North America.

Through a joint venture with two other companies, Honda has developed underlaying technology for a magnetic-coupling wireless power transfer road system (WPT road system), which will enable wireless in-motion charging of EVs, according to a press release.
Honda R&D, Taisei Corp. (Taisei), and Taisei Rotec Corp. (Taisei Rotec) plan to conduct demonstration testing of the system beginning in the Japanese 2027 fiscal year.
The system combines proprietary technology from each of the companies:
- Honda: High-power-density power receiver/transmitter units compatible with DC power distribution
- Taisei: High-response DC power supply system
- Taisei Rotec: Technology for embedding equipment in roads

“With these technologies, the system achieves high-power wireless power transfer (WPT) and excellent ease of installation in road pavement, envisioning applications for a wide range of mobility products, from passenger EVs to large commercial EVs,” the release states.

Honda says it has been working on dynamic wireless power transfer (DWPT) technology since 2021. The technology supplies power to vehicles while they are in motion and reduces the frequency of charging needed at home or at a charging station, the release states.

“Initially, Honda will strive to put DWPT technology into practical use in the logistics and transportation sectors, where DWPT technology is expected to deliver significant benefits,” the release states.

Honda, Taisei, and Taisei Rotec have been conducting research and development of the magnetic-coupling WPT road system since 2025, according to the release. This has resulted in the development of the underlaying technology for the system.

This includes conducting experiments and validation testing on a test roadway at the Future Technology Field for Taisei Group/Satte (T-FIELD/SATTE). The tests verified the effectiveness of the technologies for a WPT system, road pavement structures, and road construction methods intended for demonstration testing on public roads with large commercial vehicles, according to the release.
- DC distribution-based ground assembly (GA) systems that connect multiple GA units embedded in the road using a DC connection
- A vehicle assembly (VA) unit installed on the vehicle

Honda says that to achieve the real-world implementation of a WPT road system, it is essential to develop GA units and pavement structures with sufficient strength to withstand the loads of large commercial vehicles and a power transfer system capable of handling high-power transfer to EVs driving at high speeds, while also offering excellent practicality for installation in roads.
Testing at the T-FIELD/SATTE focused on GA units and pavement structures capable of withstanding the traffic of large vehicles with a gross vehicle weight of about 20 tons.
It also tested whether the DC power supply systems can supply high-power electricity to a DC distribution-based GA system with high responsiveness and stability.
The GA units were also tested for highly practical installation and future upgrades.

Next, the companies plan to begin testing long-term durability in late 2026 through a loading test equivalent to 1 million wheel loads using actual vehicles. It will also conduct DWPT performance tests and evaluate measures to address electromagnetic field leakage.
“Through these tests, the three companies will strive to ensure both power transfer performance and the safety of the GA units as structures embedded in the roadway,” the release states.

After this phase, the companies plan to further verify performance at high power output levels of up to 150 kW for potential application to large commercial vehicles, as well as verification of the reliability of WPT performance for vehicles traveling at high speeds.

Honda says that all three companies will participate in the “Tateyama Project” starting during the Japanese 2027 fiscal year. It will include demonstration testing of DWPT technology conducted by East Nippon Expressway Company Limited on the Tateyama Expressway in Chiba, Japan.

“Striving to realize a sustainable mobility society where people can enjoy freedom of mobility well into the future, Honda will continue to pursue co-creation with a diverse range of partners beyond the automotive industry, including road infrastructure-related businesses, government agencies and energy-related businesses,” the release states.

Gunshots erupted from solid ground towards a boat that ferried Panamanian soldier Albis Fajardo and his team during a counter-drug mission along the country’s Pacific coastline.

The team attempted to return fire as they pulled back from a harrowing effort to target a cartel leader. Fajardo, then early into his military career, felt his adrenaline surge as he realized the team had been unsuccessful: A bullet had torn through the flesh of his friend.

Over a decade later, with the early autumn sun sinking over Panamanian base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, the 47-year-old, now a first sergeant, recounted the ordeal. His friend survived, but the horror changed Fajardo’s life.
The brush with death, he said, fueled him to learn as much as he could, militarily, and eventually led him to become an instructor at the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama.

The class, offered for decades in the Central American nation before it was shuttered in 1999, has resumed in partnership between U.S. and Panamanian forces, with Panamanian service members teaching and attending the 18-day course.
As Panama’s troops have trained, lived — and in some cases, fought — in such environments, they are largely seen by U.S. personnel as the ultimate masters of the terrain.

Lt. Col. Andrew Eagen, who heads the U.S. Jungle Operations Training Center in Panama, said that as U.S. forces developed the course, they became quickly attuned to the deft tactics their Panamanian counterparts had developed for survival.
“They are the experts of this environment. We will never catch up,” he told Military Times in a mosquito-riddled interview at the jungle school.

“This does not exist in the continental United States,” he said, gesturing to the lush canopy, which was twinkling with the day’s last glimmers of sun and abuzz with the evening hum of jungle creatures. “We do not have an exposure to it. They do, and they have incredible techniques and an incredible level of comfort that the average American [does not].”
Fajardo is one of nine Panamanian instructors — from three branches of the country’s armed forces — who teach at the reestablished school.
The instructors assist in some parts of the course, but lead in areas where students learn about jungle survival, Eagen said.
In addition to the leading group, more than 10 Panamanian service members attended the course in which Military Times took part, according to Eagen.
Throughout each exercise, Panamanian troops sat interspersed with U.S. personnel and were placed in squads with a Spanish-speaking U.S. participant for course assignments.
Though the language barrier admittedly made some tactical movements difficult, U.S. personnel seemingly learned just from observing their Panamanian counterparts.

During one practical exercise, one squad had to hide in the jungle, cover their tracks to erase any disturbance to the foliage, and position themselves so they would be alerted to any incoming intruders.
The other squad’s job was to hunt down the hiding squad using tracking clues, the activity forming a tense game of tactical hide-and-seek.
The hunters ultimately won, thanks to one Panamanian squadmate who spotted a tiny vine that appeared slightly too parallel to the ground.

One rule of the jungle? Nothing is a straight line. The Panamanian student correctly identified the trailing plant, hovering inches above the muddy ground, as a hasty trip wire. Made using a vine and a piece of trash, it would have alerted the hiding squad to the hunters’ presence.

When the two groups gathered to discuss the interaction, the lanewalker found that the Panamanian student in the other squad had set up the tripwire; a particularly impressive development, considering a tripwire class was scheduled for later in the day.
During that class, an American instructor showed students how to create different forms of tripwires that could act as early warning systems. Some set off rattling cans. Others used fauna.

Before letting students practice, the instructor shared stories from Panamanian cadres who once operated in the Darién Gap, a roadless land bridge of brutally dense, remote jungle that spans 60-plus miles between Panama and Colombia and has been notoriously rife with human and drug trafficking.
Trip wires there are not historical relics of warfare from decades ago, the instructor said. Cartel members are using them now.
Several instructors, including Fajardo, have attended Panama’s own jungle school, called Panajungla.
Fajardo shook his head and shivered as he recounted the intense course in which participants were forced to survive on their own in the Teribe region of Panama’s Bocas del Toro province.
Students of the Panamanian course must shop at the “supermarket de la selva” — the jungle supermarket — to eat, using machetes to prepare or kill any nourishment they can find, Fajardo said.
Fajardo’s prized jungle delicacy is ñame, a tropical root vegetable similar to a yam. He also appreciates the taste of grubs, he said, which he likens to butter.
Tucked neatly into each Panamanian instructor’s backpack, razor-sharp machetes sat nestled in intricately carved leather coverings.

The U.S. Army teaches machete training in its jungle school, but some Panamanian instructors have attended a separate, more intensive course on using the long, daunting blade. It can clear brush, help prepare food, carve shelter and even help start a fire.
To Fajardo, it is the single most important tool for survival in the jungle. And with a smile, he jokingly referred to the machete as “mi esposa,” or my wife, in English.
To date, the U.S. Army is developing the course to dedicate at least 20 of its 120 spots to partner forces and at least 15 to Panamanians.
Though no other countries have sent soldiers yet, Eagen is confident that the school is close to having Colombian students join.

The U.S. has partnered with Colombia’s Lancero course, which is similar to Ranger School, and all three countries exchange information. Panama supports hosting Colombian forces, Eagen added, as “they have a direct relationship with the country.
“They have a lot of shared bilat right there at the Darién,” Eagen said, “so both Panamanian leaders and Colombian leaders want them to be first.”
Panama’s expertise in navigating such unforgiving terrain, meanwhile, has also prompted other countries, like Costa Rica and Brazil, to express interest in the course, Eagen said.

Other jungle courses worldwide have so far informed the new U.S. Army jungle school’s curriculum, and Eagen said the Army is designing a scenario construct for the school using threat characteristics seen by Panamanian service members.

And while Panamanian forces often confront small-team drug trafficking operations attempting to establish supply lines, Eagen was clear that the Army endeavored to replicate a potential combat environment, not the country’s security situation.

“That is not the premise of us being in Panama,” he said. “We try to make sure there are clear boundaries of understanding for the students that this is about the skills required of the environment, not about the situation in Panama.”

Though public sentiment between the countries has ebbed and flowed in the decades that followed Panama’s 1994 formal abolishment of its standing army — several years after a U.S. military invasion ousted military dictator Manuel Noriega — those tensions were absent from interactions Military Times observed among the service members during the course.

Eagen said the U.S. is mindful of the pride Panamanians take in their nation’s sovereignty. The Army, he added, has been purposeful in approaching the course’s renewed partnership with an emphasis on learning from — rather than simply teaching — its Panamanian counterparts.
